evidence: Caes. BG 1.3.4: fīliam suam in mātrimōnium dat
Plaut. Trin. 3.3.4: īre in mātrimōnium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Marriage as a state, from māter. The man takes a wife in mātrimōnium dūcere (see marry), a father gives his daughter in mātrimōnium dare or collocāre, and in mātrimōnium petere is to ask for her hand (Lewis & Short). In the plural, after Augustus, it also means wives.

terms.gloss: marriage, the union of husband and wife
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.54: prīma societās in ipsō conjugiō est
terms.comment: First any union or joining; of marriage, the bond of the couple themselves (Lewis & Short). In poetry and Tacitus also a husband or a wife (Verg. A. 3.296).

terms.gloss: marriage as a civil institution; the legal right to marry
evidence: Cic. Rep. 2.63; Liv. 4.1.1, of the right to intermarry (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Marriage regarded as a civil institution (Lewis & Short); hence the right to intermarry, which a law of the decemvirs denied between patricians and the plebs until a law of the plebs repealed it (Cic. Rep. 2.63).

phrases.latin: eīque fīliam suam in mātrimōnium dat
phrases.english: and gives him his daughter in marriage

phrases.latin: prīma societās in ipsō conjugiō est, proxima in līberīs, deinde ūna domus, commūnia omnia
phrases.english: the first bond of society is marriage itself, the next is children, then one household with everything shared

phrases.latin: Perenne conjugium animus, nōn corpus facit.
phrases.english: It is the mind, not the body, that makes a lasting marriage.

sources: Lewis & Short: matrimonium · Lewis & Short: conjugium · Lewis & Short: conubium
